lessons.title: Review — four pronouns, one slot
lessons.gloss: review — four pronouns, one slot, and the single question that chooses between them

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Nothing new in this chapter. Before the table: where does an object pronoun go?
Four chapters, four words, and now they can stand together — because you built each one separately and none of them is new here.

utterances: the one it happens to: me. pronoun: me. example: me quieres — you love me.
the one it happens to: you. pronoun: te. example: te quiero — I love you.
the one it happens to: it (masculine). pronoun: lo. example: lo tengo — I have it.
the one it happens to: it (feminine). pronoun: la. example: la hago — I make it.

segments.text: Read down the last column. The verb never moved. The pronoun never moved. Only the first word changed, and it changed for one reason at a time.
Choosing between these looks like four decisions. It is one:
Who or what is the verb landing on?
If it is you speaking becomes me.
If it is the person you are speaking to becomes te.
If it is a thing or somebody else becomes lo or la, and the noun decides which, not you.

That last clause is the whole of the difficulty. Me and te are about the conversation, so you always know them. Lo and la are about the noun, so they are only as reliable as your grip on its gender. That is why the three nouns came first: el libro and la comida are not vocabulary here so much as the two test cases you run every new pronoun against.

segments.text: Until the choice arrives before the sentence does.

segments.prompt: Name the four object pronouns you now hold.
What single question chooses between all four?
acceptedResponses: who or what the verb lands on

feedback.incorrect: Who or what the verb lands on — that is the only decision.

segments.prompt: Which two of the four depend on knowing a noun's gender?

feedback.correct: Yes — and that is where the work is.
feedback.incorrect: Lo and la. Me and te are decided by the conversation instead.

segments.text: Four pronouns — say them. (Me, te, lo, la.) Which two are decided by a noun rather than by you? (Lo and la.) Next chapter has no new forms either — it asks what these words are actually for.
